title: Attention token-sag and slew-rate analysis
content:
Summary:
This is an investigation into a reproducible throughput/latency degradation pattern we observed under realistic mixed-sequence workloads — we call it 'token-sag'. Token-sag = transient per-token throughput drop and tail-latency increase that occurs when the incoming token arrival rate changes rapidly (high slew-rate). The note compares FlashAttention, our paged-attention fallback, and a small set of fused-op paths to understand where the sag is coming from and how to mitigate it.

Why this matters:
- Customer workloads with a mix of short interactive queries and occasional long generations (chat + document completion) show intermittent latency spikes and a 10–30% per-token cost increase.
- The behavior is not steady-state queueing; it correlates with kernel selection churn, memory movement, and KV-cache warmup.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Kernel handoff hysteresis: switching between flash-paged fused kernels and fallback kernels causes short periods of inefficient memory usage and extra synchronizations.
2) Slew-rate-sensitive prefetching: our prefetch windows and KV-cache priming assume relatively stable token rates; bursts cause incomplete prefetch and extra small memcpy/launchs.
3) Small-batch fusedop degradation: fused kernels optimized for larger micro-batches drop efficiency on sub-16 token bursts.

Experiment matrix (repro steps):
- Hardware: g5x2 equivalent (A100-like), dedicated host with single process to remove multi-tenant noise.
- Models: 7B and 13B transformer (same arch), weights FP16 and Q4 variants.
- Runtimes compared: flash-fused (FlashAttention v2 fastpath), paged-attn (paged KV pipeline), fusedops-smallbatch (explicit fused attention + fused MLP), and naive reference.
- Workload generator: synthetic arrival trace with controllable slew-rate (tokens/sec ramp), mixed sequence length distribution: 60% short (8–16 tokens), 30% medium (64 tokens), 10% long (512 tokens).
- Metrics: per-token throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p95/p99 latency per request, kernel launch counts, memcpy volume, GPU occupancy snapshots, and profiler traces (nsight, CUPTI events, and our runtime tracebench).

Key commands (examples):
- run generator: ./bin/tracegen --model 7b --trace slewrate=high --mix "short:0.6,med:0.3,long:0.1" --ramp 0.1s --duration 900s
- collect traces: ./tools/collect-traces --session X --nsight --counters "sm_efficiency,gld_transactions,gst_transactions"

Observations (raw):
- At high slew-rate (ramp from 10 tokens/s to 15000 tokens/s in 100ms), flash-fused path shows immediate throughput collapse for ~40–120ms windows repeatedly (token-sag), then recovers.
- Paged-attn path shows smaller sag amplitude but longer recovery (200–500ms) and higher memcpy volume overall.
- Fusedops-smallbatch path often avoids collapse but sits at 5–12% lower peak throughput in steady state due to lower kernel vectorization.
- Kernel launch spikes align with incoming-burst edges; when bursts arrive, runtime attempts kernel switch and issues extra small kernels (many <1ms).
- KV-cache priming: when long sequences follow a series of short sequences, paged-attn issues additional page fetches resulting in 3–6 extra memcpy ops per request, contributing to tail-latency.

Profiling excerpts (human summary):
- CUPTI PM counters: sm_efficiency drops from 92% -> 55% during sag windows for flash-fused; gld/gst transactions increase 2x.
- Nsight timeline: host-spin and many small kernel launches interleaved with memcpy blocking kernels (synchronous memcpy).
- Tracebench: large variance in token time mostly explained by kernel handoffs (60%) and memcpy stalls (30%).

Controlled micro-experiments and what they revealed:
A) Increase kernel-switch debounce (simple timer heuristic):
  - Adding a 5–10ms debounce reduces the frequency of handoffs and cuts sag events in half for flash-fused, but increases average latency for some short-only workloads.
B) Prefetch window enlargement:
  - Increasing prefetch range (prefetch next N KV pages) reduces page-fault memcpys but increases memory pressure. Net: paged-attn p95 improves by ~12% in mixed trace with mild cost in occupancy.
C) Small-batch optimized fusedops:
  - A micro-kernel tuned for token counts <16 avoids the performance cliff; mixing in this kernel at runtime gave stable low-latency behavior but not the highest throughput.
D) Asynchronous memcpy and double-buffering of KV pages:
  - Convert sync memcpy to async + stream per-request to overlap page fetches with compute — reduced 3x the memcpy stall time in our traces and sm_efficiency improved by ~15% in sag windows.

Actionable recommendations (short term):
1) Implement adaptive debounce for kernel switching: base debounce on recent token inter-arrival statistics (slew-rate). Start conservative (5ms) and expose flag to tune per-deploy.
2) Add a small-batch fused attention kernel path (<16 tokens) in the kernel catalog; ensure scheduler can prefer it during short bursts.
3) Convert critical page fetch memcpy to async streams with double buffering; ensure pinned host memory for transfers to reduce CPU-GPU jitter.
4) For paged-attn, add predictive prefetch heuristic that considers sequence mix distribution (if >30% short, reduce aggressive prefetch).
5) Add a runtime telemetry signal "slew_index" (EWMA of recent token arrival rate) to expose and drive adaptive policies.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the cost tradeoff for checkpointing more KV to avoid page fetch spikes vs memory footprint? (finance / infra input needed)
- How to set defaults for debounce per customer tier? (enterprise customers with strict latency SLOs may want different policies)
- Are there lock/contention sources on the host side during async memcpy that we didn't capture? Need a host-side microbenchmark.
- Validate findings across other GPU families (H100, L4) — flash/paged kernel behavior may differ.

Next experiments planned:
- Run the async memcpy + small-batch kernel combo end-to-end on 7B and 13B across H100 and A100 to measure cross-hardware sensitivity.
- Try a control that injects synthetic tiny delays to see if kernel debounce costs outweigh gains for real customer traces.
- Run customer sample traces (with permission) to validate real-world impact; coordinate with Solutions Eng to get 2 anonymized traces.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Diego: prototype kernel-switch debounce in scheduler branch (WIP PR: GH:repo/PR#421).
- Priya: add telemetry slewrate metric to runtime and wire into Console dashboard.
- Owen: microbench host-side async memcpy, check for scheduler preemption interplay.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducibility
- Use the provided docker image: registry.redwood-inference/internal/attention-bench:202502
- Ensure GPU driver >=515 and CUDA 12.0, nsight 2024.3 for timelines.
- Run with --deterministic-off for realistic arrival jitter.

Concluding note:
Token-sag is a measurable, workload-dependent phenomenon driven by kernel handoffs, prefetch heuristics, and small-batch inefficiencies. The combination of adaptive debounce, async memcpy, and a small-batch fused kernel gives the best practical reduction in sag without sacrificing much peak throughput. This doc is a running investigation; results so far look promising but require cross-hardware validation and careful tuning before rollout to default policies.

Unresolved: prioritization and rollout plan for debounce + async memcpy across Dedicated fleets vs Hosted default.
